summary.text: A vector space is a set of vectors that can be added together and scaled by numbers, following rules called axioms.
A basis is a group of independent vectors that spans the space, and the number of vectors in any basis is the dimension.

facts.label: Scalars
facts.value: Real numbers, complex numbers, or elements of any field

facts.label: Axioms
facts.value: Addition and scaling must satisfy eight rules

facts.label: Dimension
facts.value: The number of vectors in any basis

facts.label: Subspace
facts.value: A non-empty subset closed under addition and scaling

items.prompt: A collection of arrows in the plane has a flaw: adding two of them sometimes gives an arrow outside the collection. Can it be a linear subspace?

options.label: Yes, as long as scaling works
No, a subspace must contain every sum of its members
Yes, as long as it has at least one arrow
No, a subspace may never contain nonzero arrows

items.explain: A subspace is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication, so sums and scaled versions of its members must stay inside.

items.prompt: Three arrows are such that the third is exactly the first plus the second. Are the three arrows linearly independent?

options.label: Yes, because all three are different
Yes, because each one has a direction
No, one is a combination of the others
No, because there are exactly three

items.explain: Vectors are independent only if none can be written as a linear combination of the others.

items.prompt: Two people pick different sets of basic building-block vectors (bases) for the same finite vector space. What must be true of the two sets?

options.label: They contain the same number of vectors
They share at least one vector
One is always larger than the other
They must differ by exactly one vector

items.explain: All bases of a vector space have the same cardinality, and that number is the dimension.

items.prompt: Take all polynomials, add them and scale them by numbers. How large is this vector space in dimension?

options.label: Two, since only constants and x matter
Finite, but larger than any chosen number
Zero, since polynomials are not arrows
Infinite

items.explain: Polynomial rings are countably infinite-dimensional vector spaces.

items.prompt: You list every vector you can build by scaling and adding vectors from a chosen group G. What have you built?

options.label: The span of G, the smallest subspace holding G
A basis of the whole space that G lives in
The scalars that every vector of G uses
The dimension number belonging to the group G

items.explain: The span of G is the set of all linear combinations of G, and it is the smallest subspace containing G.

items.prompt: Which measurement is best modeled by a Euclidean vector?

options.label: The temperature in a room
The number of seats in a room
The age of a person in a room
The velocity of a ball rolling across a room

items.explain: Euclidean vectors model quantities such as forces and velocity that have a direction as well as a magnitude.

right.label: The smallest subspace containing a group of vectors
A vector built by scaling and adding chosen vectors
The number of vectors in any basis
Independent vectors that span the whole space

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A vector space is a set whose members, called vectors, can be added to one another and scaled by multiplying them with numbers. Those numbers are called scalars. Adding and scaling must obey a list of rules known as the vector axioms, and the formal definition lists eight of them. Every sum of two vectors, and every scaled vector, is again a vector in the same space.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing the scalars
paragraphs.text: The kind of scalars you allow decides the kind of vector space you get. With real numbers as scalars it is a real vector space, and with complex numbers it is a complex vector space. These two are the most common. More generally, the scalars can come from any field F, and the result is called a vector space over F.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Vector spaces generalize Euclidean vectors, which are used to model physical quantities such as force and velocity that have a direction as well as a size. Together with matrices, which let you compute inside vector spaces, they are the foundation of linear algebra. That pairing gives a compact way to handle and study systems of linear equations.

paragraphs.heading: Combinations and independence
paragraphs.text: A linear combination is what you get by scaling several vectors and adding the results, as in a₁𝐠₁ + a₂𝐠₂ + ⋯ + aₖ𝐠ₖ. The scaling numbers are called its coefficients. A group of vectors is linearly independent when none of them can be written as a linear combination of the others. Put another way, the only combination of them that gives the zero vector is the one where every coefficient is zero.

paragraphs.heading: Subspaces and span
paragraphs.text: A subspace is a non-empty part of a vector space that is closed: adding two of its vectors, or scaling one, never leads outside it. The span of a set of vectors is the smallest subspace that contains them all. It is also the set of every linear combination of those vectors. If the span of a set is a space W, the set is said to generate W.

paragraphs.heading: Basis and dimension
paragraphs.text: A basis is a set of vectors that is linearly independent and also spans the whole space. Every vector space has at least one basis, and usually many. All the bases of one space have the same size, and that size is called the dimension. Roughly, the dimension counts the independent directions in the space. A space is finite-dimensional when its dimension is a natural number, and infinite-dimensional otherwise.

paragraphs.heading: What dimension tells you
paragraphs.text: Two vector spaces over the same field with the same dimension are isomorphic: every property that depends only on their vector-space structure is exactly the same. Finite-dimensional spaces turn up naturally in geometry. Infinite-dimensional ones appear in many parts of mathematics. Polynomial rings, for example, are vector spaces whose dimension is countably infinite.
